courses.title: Personal & Professional Development
courses.contribution: Academic writing, literature evaluation, self-reflection and work with a societal partner support general academic and professional development.

evidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
evidence.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
evidence.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

courses.title: Introduction to Sociology
courses.contribution: Classical and critical sociological theory connects solidarity, identity and social boundaries to class, race, gender and migration.

evidence.profile: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.
evidence.topics: Sociological imagination and knowledge; Social structure and socialization; Classical social theory; Colonialism and the formation of sociology; Solidarity and modernity; Identity, belonging and othering; Groups and social networks; Capital, class and mobility; Race and gender inequality; Global inequality and migration; Education and labour-market inequality
evidence.methods: Theory-guided sociological case analysis; Comparative analysis of sociological perspectives; Library-based social-science research; Sociological research-question formulation

courses.title: Modern History
courses.contribution: Historical inquiry into industrialisation, empire, migration and decolonisation supplies context for global cultural change.

evidence.profile: Surveys economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present while questioning the meaning and periodization of modernity. Students examine industrialization, political ideologies, nationalism, imperialism, migration, world wars, revolution, decolonization, the Cold War and globalization. Historical research and essays connect specific questions to evidence. A group project analyzes historical visions of the future as products of their own contexts and compares them with subsequent developments.
evidence.topics: Modernity and periodization; Industrialization and reform; Political ideologies and nationalism; Migration and imperialism; National, class, gender and racial identities; World wars; Russian Revolution and Soviet history; Democracy and dictatorship; Cold War; Decolonization; Globalization; Historical visions of the future
evidence.methods: Historical contextualization; Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Source triangulation; Historical research-question development

courses.title: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
courses.contribution: Written argument, speeches, rhetorical analysis and storytelling develop tools for communicating social inquiry.

evidence.profile: Teaches rhetorical analysis and persuasive communication through classical history, theory and practice. Students study Greek and Roman rhetoric, the five canons, types of discourse, persuasive appeals, argumentation and fallacies. Written exercises, debates and public speeches develop invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. An applied project creates narrative and storytelling material for an immersive educational setting concerned with Zeeland's climate and community.
evidence.topics: Greek and Roman rhetoric; Deliberative, forensic and epideictic discourse; Logos, ethos and pathos; Invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery; Argumentation and fallacies; Tropes and schemes; Stasis and enthymemes; Persuasive speech; Narrative and storytelling; Immersive educational communication
evidence.methods: Rhetorical text analysis; Stasis analysis; Argument invention and arrangement; Stylistic analysis and composition; Structured debate; Persuasive speechwriting and delivery; Educational storytelling design

courses.title: Qualitative Research Methodology
courses.contribution: Interviews, ethnographic observation, documentary and visual methods, ethics and coding support empirical qualitative inquiry.

evidence.profile: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
evidence.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination
evidence.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation

courses.title: Histories of Gender
courses.contribution: Primary sources, interviews and storytelling develop gender and sexuality history through North American cases and public history.

evidence.profile: Studies gendered histories and lives in North America from the nineteenth century to the present, centering storytelling and intersectionality. Queer and heteronormative narratives connect slavery, family, sexuality, health, incarceration and contemporary backlash to resistance and activism. Students interpret primary sources and scholarship, interview older queer people, contribute to the Walking with Pride activist artwork, and conduct an original research project in a chosen format.
evidence.topics: Gender and intersectionality; Body sovereignty; Heteronormativity and compulsory heterosexuality; Homonationalism; Rainbow capitalism; Masculinity and sexuality; Queer ageing and memory; Slavery and racialized gender histories; Family and socialization; Health and pathologization; Media bias and book bans; Incarceration; Queer activism and resistance
evidence.methods: Historical primary-source research; Intersectional analysis; Oral-history interviewing; Critical interpretation of memoir and cultural representations; Arts-based research; Community-engaged activist art; Reflective analysis

courses.title: Introduction to World Archaeology
courses.contribution: Comparative analysis of artefacts, production and identity supplies material-culture methods across Europe, Asia and Africa.

evidence.profile: Examines how making objects shaped communities and identities from the Neolithic through antiquity across Europe, Asia and Africa. Artefacts, production technologies and craft organization are interpreted in relation to social status, religion, gender, exchange and environmental settings. Students produce an archaeological catalogue description and technical drawings, research a craft-related question and design a hands-on educational game. A small contemporary-archaeology project collects local material evidence and proposes a testable interpretation.
evidence.topics: Materiality, craft and cognition; Settlement and landscape; Neolithic and Bronze Age communities; Craft production and social hierarchy; Trade and exchange; Pottery and iconography; Seals, textiles and elite identities; Domestic and urban craft spaces; Archaeological interpretation; Ancient technology and community identity; Contemporary archaeology
evidence.methods: Artefact observation, measurement and cataloguing; Archaeological technical drawing; Visual and stylistic analysis; Comparative material-culture analysis; Archaeological database and literature research; Material-evidence-based argumentation; Archaeological educational-game design; Contemporary archaeological data collection and hypothesis development

courses.title: Ethics
courses.contribution: Moral theories and case argument provide ethical reasoning that can inform research responsibilities.

evidence.profile: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
evidence.topics: Divine command and human nature; Moral relativism and universalism; Utilitarianism and consequentialism; Kantian ethics; Virtue ethics; Social contract and intuitionism; Feminist and care ethics; Nietzschean genealogy and nihilism; Murdoch's sovereignty of good; Moral value and perspective; Death, absurdity and meaning; Ethical theory and practical judgment
evidence.methods: Close philosophical text analysis; Reconstruction and critical evaluation of moral arguments; Comparison of ethical theories; Conceptual analysis; Independent philosophical argument development

courses.title: Modern Sociology
courses.contribution: Critical, decolonial and intersectional social theory develops analysis of modernity, inequality and disciplinary exclusions.

evidence.profile: Examines twentieth-century and contemporary social theory alongside critical accounts of modernity, colonialism and disciplinary exclusion. Functionalism, critical theory, Black feminist thought, phenomenology, symbolic interactionism and Bourdieu's work are read with postcolonial, decolonial and Indigenous perspectives. Students compare theories and apply them to empirical cases, including visual material. An individual research paper develops a theoretically grounded interpretation of a selected social phenomenon.
evidence.topics: Modernity and Eurocentrism; Functionalism; Frankfurt School critical theory; Black feminist thought and intersectionality; Social construction of reality; Symbolic interactionism; Stigma and othering; Social space, capital and art; Coloniality and postcolonialism; Decolonial and Indigenous sociology; Gender and power
evidence.methods: Close reading of social theory; Comparative theoretical analysis; Theory-guided empirical case analysis; Visual sociological analysis; Literature-based sociological research

courses.title: History of Empires
courses.contribution: Comparative historical cases investigate imperial ideology, governance, culture and legacies.

evidence.profile: Examines empires comparatively across global history, from ancient Persia, Rome and China to early-modern and modern imperial powers and contemporary claims to imperial status. Students analyze expansion, administration, military and economic systems, legitimacy, ideology, culture, decline and legacies. The course combines theories of empire with historically specific cases, historiographical discussion, source analysis and an independently developed research essay.
evidence.topics: Concepts and theories of empire; Imperial rise, expansion and decline; Administration and succession; Military and economic structures; Imperial ideologies and legitimacy; Culture and empire; Ancient and medieval empires; European overseas empires; Modern Asian and Eurasian empires; American power; Contemporary and future empires; Imperial legacies
evidence.methods: Comparative historical analysis; Historiographical analysis; Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Historical research-question development

courses.title: Foundations of Comparative Politics
courses.contribution: Comparative political analysis investigates institutions, participation and democratic change through operationalised measures.

evidence.profile: Introduces empirical comparison of political systems, with democracy, democratization and autocratization as central concerns. Students study political institutions, rules, actors and behaviour, including parties, elections, participation, polarization, interest groups and policy. Research exercises operationalize and measure democracy using V-Dem data and compare academic literature-search tools. A qualitative or quantitative research memo answers a theoretically grounded comparative-politics question through empirical analysis.
evidence.topics: Democracy and authoritarianism; Democratization and democratic backsliding; States, nations and nationalism; Constitutions and courts; Executives, legislatures and bureaucracies; Political economy; Parties and party systems; Populism and technocracy; Elections and electoral systems; Political culture and polarization; Political participation; Interest groups and public policy
evidence.methods: Theory-driven qualitative and quantitative research; Concept operationalization and democracy measurement; V-Dem data analysis; Comparative case analysis; Academic literature searching with OpenAlex and AI tools; Empirical election analysis; Research-question formulation

courses.title: Media & Race
courses.contribution: Visual and audio evidence, archives and podcast production support study of racialisation and representation.

evidence.profile: Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture. Theatre, photographs, news, film, music, tourism and literature reveal both oppression and resistance. Students investigate exclusion, racialized bodies, youth, marginalized storytelling and imagined futures. Participant observation, archival research, a documentary podcast and a cross-cultural Photo/Voice project connect historical analysis with lived experience and representation.
evidence.topics: Racial construction and whiteness; Media, power and representation; Leisure, tourism and racial identity; Crime, punishment and the racialized body; Asian-American exclusion; Japanese-American incarceration; Childhood and youth; Marginalized and Indigenous storytelling; Racial extremism and propaganda; Alienation and community; Food, environment and cultural nourishment; Afrofuturism and Indigenous futurisms
evidence.methods: Participant observation; Archival primary-source research; Historical media analysis; Documentary podcast research, scripting and audio production; Photo/Voice photography and audio narrative; Cross-cultural interpretive reflection

courses.title: Theory of International Relations
courses.contribution: Theories and cases of international relations develop analysis of conflict, colonial relations and climate politics.

evidence.profile: Introduces international relations and geopolitics through competing theoretical approaches and historical and contemporary cases. Students study realism, liberalism, Marxism, constructivism, critical theory and foreign-policy analysis. Case research connects theories to conflicts, colonial relationships, economic competition and climate politics. A UN Security Council simulation requires country-position research, strategy and position papers, negotiation and collaborative resolution drafting.
evidence.topics: International state system and non-state actors; Classical and contemporary geopolitics; Realism and neorealism; Liberalism and neoliberalism; Marxism and world-systems theory; Constructivism and critical theory; Foreign-policy decision-making; War and great-power competition; Colonialism and economic relations; Climate politics; UN Security Council diplomacy
evidence.methods: Theory-guided international case analysis; Historical-source analysis; Comparative foreign-policy analysis; Country-position and strategy research; Diplomatic negotiation simulation; Position-paper and resolution drafting

courses.title: African Art & Heritage
courses.contribution: Western African visual traditions, museums and restitution connect material culture to regional histories and colonial power.

evidence.profile: Introduces African art and heritage with particular attention to western African visual traditions and their cultural, religious and social meanings. Students study sculpture, masks and other forms across regional contexts before tracing African art's role in European modernism, the Harlem Renaissance and African artistic renewal. Colonial dispossession, museum collecting and restitution form a major later strand. An independent paper develops a research question supported by scholarly evidence.

courses.title: Style & Meaning
courses.contribution: Stylistic analysis examines how linguistic choices, discourse and cognition shape interpretation.

evidence.profile: Studies how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts but also in nonfiction. Students connect linguistic description to interpretation across grammar, discourse and cognition. Stylistic frameworks address foregrounding, dialogue, narration, modality, transitivity, deixis, schemas, construal and text worlds. Frequent analysis exercises lead to an original, research-supported stylistic analysis of a selected text.

evidence.methods: Linguistic stylistic analysis; Close textual analysis; Discourse and conversation analysis; Speech and thought presentation analysis; Modality and transitivity analysis; Deictic and cognitive-grammar analysis; Text-world analysis; Framework-based interpretation supported by retrievable textual evidence

courses.title: Social Psychology
courses.contribution: Empirical research on social influence, prejudice and group processes adds behavioural perspectives on social life.

evidence.profile: Introduces the scientific study of how thoughts, feelings and behaviour are shaped by other people and social situations. Social cognition, the self, influence and persuasion lead into group processes, prejudice, aggression, prosocial behaviour, attraction and close relationships. Students critically examine empirical research, synthesize findings from journal articles, formulate theory-guided questions and design a feasible study. The final project proposes research rather than conducting an empirical investigation.
evidence.topics: Social cognition and person perception; The self and self-motives; Social influence; Persuasion, attitudes and behaviour; Group processes; Prejudice, stereotyping and discrimination; Prejudice reduction; Interpersonal aggression; Prosocial behaviour; Interpersonal attraction and close relationships
evidence.methods: Critical appraisal of empirical social-psychology research; Literature synthesis; Theory-guided hypothesis formulation; Research design for a proposed social-psychology study

courses.title: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
courses.contribution: Civil-society theory and independent research address trust, public spheres, solidarity and social movements.

evidence.profile: Focuses on civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theory. Students examine social trust, capital, hegemony, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair across political and regional contexts. An experience report relates personal engagement or observation to course concepts. An individual research project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyze a civil-society organization, movement, initiative or related phenomenon.

courses.title: Introduction to Political Philosophy
courses.contribution: Political texts and essays develop analysis of authority, rights and normative accounts of social organisation.

evidence.profile: Surveys political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers. Students examine views of human nature, society, rights and authority in their historical contexts and compare their proposed solutions with current political problems. Close study of original texts, an individual essay and a group project developing a coherent political philosophy connect historical interpretation to normative argument.

courses.title: European Union Politics
courses.contribution: Empirical coding of parliamentary amendments supports analysis of representation and institutions in Europe.

evidence.profile: Studies EU institutions, political actors, integration and policymaking, linking formal rules to current political issues. Students analyze representation, legitimacy, interests, agenda setting, decision-making and implementation. A substantial empirical project examines European Parliament committee amendments, connecting MEP ideology and possible interest-group influence to amendment activity. Students develop a project plan, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.

courses.title: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
courses.contribution: Human-rights law and political philosophy provide institutional and ethical context for inequality and citizenship.

evidence.profile: Studies human rights both as positive law and as philosophical claims. Students examine the UDHR, European and UN protection systems, monitoring institutions and landmark cases alongside natural law, natural rights, legal positivism and critiques of universality. Historical and philosophical texts frame debates about dignity, life and reproductive rights, punishment, religious freedom, expression and democracy. Close engagement with legal and philosophical arguments supports independent moral positions.

courses.title: Peace & Conflict
courses.contribution: Interdisciplinary research on conflict, identity, structural inequality and colonial legacies supports analysis of development and peace.

evidence.profile: Examines causes and dynamics of conflict and approaches to peace through legal, sociological, political and historical perspectives. Structural inequality, identity and colonial legacies are connected to international security, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice. Students compare travelling concepts across disciplines, produce an interdisciplinary podcast, and develop an evidence-based policy brief with a research dossier. Positionality reflection addresses how assumptions shape inquiry.

courses.title: Researching the “American Century”
courses.contribution: A substantial historical research paper develops question formulation, source criticism and methodological reasoning.

evidence.description2: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.

courses.title: The Documentary
courses.contribution: Documentary analysis and production connect visual evidence, representation, ethics and social context.

evidence.profile: Studies documentary history, modes and styles alongside practical documentary production. Students analyze nonfiction representation in historical, social, ethical and aesthetic contexts, from early and Soviet filmmaking through direct cinema and contemporary forms. Topics include propaganda, advocacy, ethnography, history, nature, audio and interactive documentary. Production workshops guide a short film through preproduction, filming and postproduction, with reflection on interviewing and representational choices.

courses.title: Perspectives on Literary Meaning
courses.contribution: A research project compares literary interpretations using perspectives such as feminist, Marxist and minority approaches.

evidence.description2: Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.

courses.title: Sustainability Essentials I
courses.contribution: Planetary boundaries, uncertainty, modelling and physical principles explain material dimensions of environmental change.

evidence.profile: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.

evidence.methods: Graph interpretation and comparison; Fermi estimation; Difference-equation and first-order linear differential-equation modelling; Elementary differentiation and integration; Biopolymer preparation; Strength and elasticity measurement; Iterative experimental improvement

courses.title: Climate Change
courses.contribution: Climate science, impacts, adaptation and mitigation provide context for climate justice and governance.

evidence.profile: Introduces climate-change science, societal impacts, and mitigation and adaptation. Students examine greenhouse gases, feedbacks, tipping points, ocean acidification and sea-level rise, then consequences for ecosystems, agriculture, transport, buildings and health. Climate justice, governance, communication and misinformation connect physical changes to social responses. Solution pathways include energy systems, carbon removal and climate-adaptive planning. Students interview a stakeholder and produce a short film, alongside reflection on their own role.

evidence.methods: Stakeholder interviewing; Short-film production for climate communication; Source-credibility evaluation; What? So What? Now What? reflective model

courses.title: Sustainability Essentials II
courses.contribution: Waves, chemistry and materials work add scientific context for evaluating sustainability claims.

evidence.profile: Connects wave physics, chemistry and materials science to sustainability questions. Students study wave behaviour and observation methods, chemical analysis, microscopic material structure and macroscopic stress and strain. Practical sessions include wave applications and chemistry laboratory work. Reflective inquiries and a final project critically assess sustainability campaigns, identify greenwashing and communicate evidence-based improvements to a public audience.

courses.title: Governance of Sustainability
courses.contribution: Cases of environmental governance and a Zeeland study relate institutions, participation, power and policy to collective environmental decisions.

evidence.profile: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.

evidence.methods: Governance-framework application; Problem diagnosis and causal analysis; Stakeholder and policy-option matrices; Policy evaluation; Policy-advice memo development; Stakeholder and expert interviewing; Comparative analysis of normative policy perspectives

courses.title: Communicating the Climate Crisis
courses.contribution: Climate discourse and protest media analysis develop practical interpretation of public environmental arguments.

evidence.description2: Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate.

courses.title: Media & the Environment
courses.contribution: Environmental media analysis connects images, narratives, contested knowledge and public ecological debate.

evidence.profile: Examines how visual, audiovisual, sound and digital media shape understanding of ecological problems and human-nonhuman relations. Environmental-humanities concepts guide close analysis of images, narratives and aesthetic strategies across cultural and historical contexts. Students investigate how scientific knowledge, risk and lived experience become representations that influence ethics, public debate and sustainability. A final analytical paper or media-based project develops an argument grounded in course theory.

courses.title: Ecosystems Uncovered: How Nature Works
courses.contribution: Population and ecosystem ecology supplies an empirical basis for understanding ecological change.

evidence.profile: Develops ecological principles from organisms and populations to communities and ecosystems. Environmental conditions, resources and life cycles frame competition, feeding relationships, selection, population dynamics and biodiversity. Energy and matter cycles connect ecological processes to conservation and human impacts. Dedicated practical sessions teach simple ecological modelling in R, and a small research project communicates findings through a poster.

courses.title: Environmental Biogeochemistry
courses.contribution: Geochemical laboratory and modelling work explain environmental processes relevant to remediation and resource recovery.

evidence.profile: Examines chemical and biological controls on near-surface Earth systems, especially interactions among water, minerals, rocks and soils. Students study aqueous composition, equilibrium, speciation, carbonate and redox chemistry, adsorption, weathering and biomineralization. Laboratory investigations and geochemical modelling connect these processes to contaminant behaviour, wastewater treatment, remediation and resource recovery. A project applies geochemical principles to a current environmental issue.

courses.title: Building with Nature
courses.contribution: Zeeland cases and an intervention proposal show how ecosystem-based design connects infrastructure and coastal adaptation.

evidence.profile: Introduces approaches that combine human infrastructure with natural processes and ecosystem health, with particular attention to Zeeland and the history of water management on Walcheren. Students examine applications across sandy and muddy coasts, lowland lakes, rivers and estuaries, cities and ports. Projects investigate ecological connectivity and formulate a Building with Nature intervention; a practical wall-building project explores constructed structures.

courses.title: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
courses.contribution: Social movement theory and environmental justice cases examine contested transitions and civic engagement.

evidence.description2: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.

courses.title: Introduction to Film & Media
courses.contribution: Close analysis of moving images, editing, sound and spectatorship supports visual interpretation and media history.

evidence.profile: Introduces how moving images create meaning through cinematography, editing, sound, mise-en-scène, narrative and performance. Film history connects early cinema, Expressionism, montage, Hollywood and New Waves to feminist and postcolonial interpretation. Broader media topics include television, digital platforms, representation and spectatorship. An independent analytical or creative-analytical project combines close analysis, theory, scholarly research and, where chosen, original media work.

courses.title: Modern Art & Modern Museums
courses.contribution: Museum and exhibition analysis examines curatorial framing and Eurocentric narratives through evidence-based art history.

evidence.profile: Examines modern and contemporary art from the late nineteenth century to the present together with the institutions that shape its display and reception. Students study avant-gardes, abstraction, modernist design, figuration, postmodern and conceptual practices, and global contemporary art. Museums, exhibitions, curatorial choices and Eurocentric narratives are treated critically. An independently researched paper develops a focused art-historical question, methods and evidence-based argument.
evidence.topics: Modernism and avant-gardes; Cubism and abstraction; Modern architecture and design; Figuration and Mexican muralism; Abstract Expressionism; Minimalism and Pop Art; Postmodernism and conceptual art; Photography, installation, performance and video art; Globalization and contemporary art; Authorship, originality and medium; Museums, curating and reception; Eurocentrism in art history
evidence.methods: Art-historical interpretation and contextual analysis; Critical analysis of museums and curatorial practices; Scholarly literature review; Independent art-historical research

courses.title: Introduction to Data Science
courses.contribution: Cleaning, analysing and visualising tabular, textual and spatial data in R gives practical quantitative tools.

evidence.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
evidence.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
evidence.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis

courses.title: Native American Histories
courses.contribution: Indigenous histories and collaborative public-history work explore representation, reciprocity and institutional violence.

evidence.profile: Studies Native American social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present through Indigenous perspectives and collaborative inquiry. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to contemporary resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, relational accountability and reciprocity inform work with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders. Arts-based collaborations and a public-history project develop respectful, accessible accounts of historical and contemporary issues.
evidence.topics: Indigenous histories and ways of knowing; Colonialism and white saviourism; Indian wars; Boarding schools and childhood trauma; Institutional confinement; Adoption and blood quantum; Gendered violence and missing Indigenous people; Traditional ecological knowledge; Food sovereignty; Decolonization and Indigenization; Cultural resistance and resurgence; Indigenous storytelling and public history
evidence.methods: Indigenous storywork and relational historical inquiry; Primary-source and oral-history analysis; Arts-based collaborative inquiry; Photo/Voice photography and audio narratives; Historical contextualization of contemporary issues; Public-history multimedia production

alternatives.label: Culture, Society & Global Change
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum visibly combines culture, society, identity, global change and qualitative inquiry without implying a dedicated ethnographic fieldwork degree.
alternatives.concept: Study identity, inequality and cultural change through sociology, comparative history, politics and material culture. Qualitative inquiry, source criticism and documentary production give you different ways to investigate how people organise social life.
progression: The schedule has 24 distinct courses and 7 advanced courses. First-year personal and professional development, planned offerings and formal prerequisites pass the current workbook checks.

alternatives.label: Ecology, Communities & Global Change
alternatives.labelReason: The curriculum combines social and cultural analysis with climate, sustainability, ecology and community responses to global change.
alternatives.concept: Study how communities and institutions respond to environmental change. Sociology, qualitative research and environmental governance connect with climate science, ecology, coastal adaptation and the public communication of environmental issues.
progression: The schedule has 24 distinct courses and 8 advanced courses. First-year personal and professional development, planned offerings and formal prerequisites pass the current workbook checks.
alternatives.distinctness: This route has 10 distinct courses compared with route 1, 10 distinct courses compared with route 3. Its central application and associated coursework distinguish it from both other routes.

alternatives.label: Visual Culture, Media & Social Inquiry
alternatives.concept: Study how images, institutions and media shape representation, identity and social action. Film, documentary production, museum studies and historical inquiry connect with sociology, qualitative methods and introductory text and spatial data analysis.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum combines cultural and social theory with film, media, visual inquiry, politics and data analysis; the label states those visible strands directly.
progression: The schedule has 24 distinct courses and 7 advanced courses. First-year personal and professional development, planned offerings and formal prerequisites pass the current workbook checks.
alternatives.distinctness: This route has 6 distinct courses compared with route 1, 10 distinct courses compared with route 2. Its central application and associated coursework distinguish it from both other routes.
